item.title: Most recombinant collagen is just soft rope without triple helix structure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-bizthisway-多数重组胶原蛋白只是一条软绳-没有三螺旋结构就不算真正起效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-bizthisway-多数重组胶原蛋白只是一条软绳-没有三螺旋结构就不算真正起效/
item.description: Many commercial recombinant collagens produce only a single amino acid chain that never folds into the triple helix structure needed to fit into cellular receptors and function. This—not marketing differences—is the real technical moat.
item.content:encoded:
Many commercial recombinant collagens produce only a single amino acid chain that never folds into the triple helix structure needed to fit into cellular receptors and function. This—not marketing differences—is the real technical moat.

The first half covers foundational difficulty in protein structure research and what AI actually does—high information density. The middle section on collagen's triple helix, the Korean customer visit, and the unexpected wrinkle reduction finding contain the most valuable business insights; worth listening through completely.

10:34 Protein folding has more possibilities than all particles in the observable universe
Zhang Ying (张颖) offered a concrete comparison: break down everything visible in the observable universe into atoms and you get roughly 10^80; but a protein with hundreds of amino acids has 20 to the power of several hundred possible arrangements from pure combinatorics, a number larger than all atoms in the universe. This means protein structure cannot be solved by brute-force computation, explaining why this field has advanced slowly for decades—not because technology is crude, but because the problem's combinatorial space is more terrifying than the cosmos.

15:27 AI predicts protein structures, but prediction is just the starting line
He emphasized that prediction and experimental verification are two different things: prediction is like a blindfolded artist being described what to draw—they can get the outline but never the details; experimental verification is actual photography and reconstruction. Even with DeepMind, accuracy improved from 30-40% to 90%, but that's just obtaining a rough model; work then returns to the lab for validation. He also noted DeepMind's team has disbanded within Google, with Hassabis starting Isomorphic to focus on drug pipelines, suggesting these tools' real value lies in the first 5-10% of drug development, not the finish line.

27:13 Animal-derived collagen is being eliminated for ethics and safety together
The industry long extracted collagen from pigs, cattle, and other animals, but Zhang noted that cosmetics giants like L'Oréal and Shiseido established animal-free, chemical-free strategies over a decade ago. One reason is ethical—unwillingness to kill animals for extraction. The other is safety: poor quality control of animal materials risks introducing animal pathogens into human bodies, risks nearly impossible to fully eliminate in production. This ensures recombinant protein technology using fermentation to make human-sequence collagen will gradually replace animal extraction.

29:14 Structure determines function; without it, a protein isn't a protein
Zhang explained why Liying (丽颖) chose Tri-Helix as its brand name: there are 28 types of collagen in the human body, but all their functional regions must exist in triple helix form to fit into cellular surface receptors like puzzle pieces and transmit signals. Most recombinant collagen on the market is just soft polypeptide chain without this spatial structure, so there's an industry saying—‘without structure, it's at best just a polypeptide chain, it doesn't actually work.’

35:16 Korea's largest cosmetics group screened hundreds of companies before them
Korea's #1 beauty conglomerate and #1 medical aesthetics company invited Zhang to visit, where he learned they had tried cross-linked hyaluronic acid a decade prior but abandoned it for poor results. This time they screened roughly 400-500 related companies in China through a third-party consulting firm, narrowed to 5-6 for site visits, nearly gave up—and found Liying at the final stop. The critical factor: their CTO had biochemistry training and understood protein must emphasize structure; every other company failed to clearly explain and convince them about ‘triple helix structure.’

41:54 During hair growth testing they accidentally discovered wrinkles shrank
Liying initially focused all literature and animal experiments on hair growth signaling pathways. After a partner's chairman tried it, third-party safety testing unexpectedly found test subjects' wrinkles decreased nearly 40% in one month. The team then tested on employees across age groups and found obvious improvements in pores and fine lines—because poor cellular environments (such as from cheap petrochemical skincare ingredients irritating cells) make pore cells enlarge, while collagen makes cells healthier, shrinking pores. This unexpected discovery prompted the team to pivot toward the skincare market.

46:18 They quit pure ingredient sales and built their own brand instead
Liying initially planned to sell materials to major cosmetics brands as a supply-chain partner, but Zhang did the math: selling raw materials has limited scale, hitting ceiling around 10 million in revenue, and brands won't prioritize your ingredient, diluting its unique value. He believes good technology must become good product to preserve pricing power, otherwise technology gets ‘drowned in a mediocre product.’ This was the core logic behind his decision to launch the Tri-Helix brand himself.

54:41 At 31 with British permanent residency, he fled a predictable life
Zhang obtained British permanent residency at 31 in 2017, but six months later felt bored—he could see the next 20, 30 years of his life laid out and wanted to escape that certainty. Combined with post-Brexit decline in UK standing, his father suffering health scares needing care, and China's biotech gap with the West still substantial, this pushed him to start a company back home rather than continue deep lab work on protein structure alone.

item.title: The real money in K-Beauty is not in brands, but in contract manufacturers and distributors
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-sv101-韩妆真正赚钱的不是品牌-而是代工厂和分销商/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-sv101-韩妆真正赚钱的不是品牌-而是代工厂和分销商/
item.description: Korean beauty brands excel at making consumers feel their products work, but what truly endures across cycles is the contract manufacturers like Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) who produce them, and distributors like Olive Young and Silicon2 who stock them—the brands themselves are more like fireworks, each one bursting and then moving to the next.
item.content:encoded:
Korean beauty brands excel at making consumers feel their products work, but what truly endures across cycles is the contract manufacturers like Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) who produce them, and distributors like Olive Young and Silicon2 who stock them—the brands themselves are more like fireworks, each one bursting and then moving to the next.

For anyone who wants to understand brand strategies and industry chain division of labor; the mid-section comparing R&D processes across China, Korea and Europe is somewhat lengthy, with core insights concentrated in the second half.

15:14 Korean beauty shifted from brand-driven to product-driven sales
In the 1.0 era, brands like Sulwhasoo and Innisfree operated on ‘brand-to-product’ leverage: consumers remembered the brand and bought whatever it sold. In 2.0, it reversed to ‘product-to-brand’: consumers remember product nicknames like ‘little yellow oil’or ‘flight attendant spray’but can't recall the brand behind them—and the brand doesn't expect them to. With short-form video attention spans at two or three seconds, blowing up a single product pays better than building brand equity.

20:16 APR built the highest K-Beauty market cap with one spray
Among Korea's new beauty giants, APR (parent of Medicube), founded in 2014, is now Korea's highest-valued beauty company, surpassing legacy Amorepacific. International sales account for 80%, of which approximately 30% from the US. Another contender, Goodai Global, began as a distributor and parlayed its success distributing Beauty of Joseon into acquiring brands. Its sales grew from 100 million won to 1.4 trillion won (approximately $1 billion) in just years—the company filed for IPO this month.

24:17 The THAAD crisis forced an unexpected Korean beauty pivot to global markets
Korean beauty brands that emerged between 2014–2016 initially targeted the Chinese market, where resellers could profit over 200,000 yuan per month. The 2017 THAAD incident abruptly closed China's door, but these young brands—still small enough to be agile—exited China immediately and pivoted to Southeast Asia and Western markets. Ironically, this reversal let them globalize faster than legacy brands already running dozens of stores in China; what could have been a disaster became, in Leng Xiao's phrase, an unexpected alignment of timing, geography, and circumstance.

34:23 Three major brands' identical eye patches exposed contract manufacturing dependency risks
In September, Fenty Beauty, Huda Beauty, and Glow Recipe each launched nearly identical ‘slice eye patches’ within the same week, each accusing the others of copying—until it emerged they all sourced their ‘proprietary technology’ directly from the same Korean contract manufacturer. Cosmax (科丝美诗) and Kolmar (科玛) are no longer simple manufacturers; they handle everything from product design to regulatory compliance, making Korean brands astonishingly fast at launching new products. But this structural advantage creates structural vulnerability: product homogenization across brands becomes virtually inevitable.

46:34 Korean beauty excels at performing efficacy, not achieving it
Beauty consumers globally demand efficacy, but ‘making it feel effective’and ‘actually being effective’are different things. Chinese brands focused on serious R&D—like Youshiyan (优时颜) with peptide products or Juzi Shengwu (巨子生物) with collagen—may deliver more robust efficacy but struggle to explain it clearly. Korean brands took ‘efficacy theatre’ to an extreme: through ritual-heavy product designs like micro-needle bottles, flight attendant sprays, and jelly patches you twist apart, they create strong visual and tactile feedback. The long-term efficacy median may actually be lower than brands doing rigorous R&D, but the perception wins.

1:01:45 K-pop, K-Food, and K-Beauty were written into the same national policy
After the 1997 Asian financial crisis, Korea's government elevated cultural exports to national strategy through the Framework Act on the Promotion of the Cultural Industry. K-Drama, K-pop, K-Food, and K-Beauty were then deliberately synchronized: TV dramas repeatedly featured fried chicken and beer, K-pop idols ‘naturally’ used Korean beauty products in behind-the-scenes variety show footage, and BTS members' use of Mediheal sheet masks and sunscreen once directly boosted sales. These four pillars work together to amplify Korea's overall cultural reach globally.

1:22:57 Acquiring Korean beauty brands means buying a windfall, not future capability
L'Oréal's acquisition of 3CE mirrors Estée Lauder's botched play with Dijiyating (蒂佳婷)—the company considered selling it, then bought it back. Both cases reveal the same problem: international conglomerates acquire Korean brands at peak hype, capturing near-term upside rather than sustained growth. Korean brands excel at launching fireworks—constant novelty—but rarely sustain a single long-running product. Once absorbed into a multinational's ESG-compliant, diversity-focused corporate system, they lose the scrappy execution that drove their rise.

1:26:40 Chinese beauty brands have deep roots but lack the storytelling canopy
A brand or industry resembles a tree: the unseen roots are R&D, raw materials, and foundational research; the trunk is organization and distribution; the canopy is marketing and brand narrative. Korean brands' strength lies almost entirely in the canopy; their roots and trunk may not be more solid than China's. Chinese beauty has already reached the global first tier in foundational research and efficacy—the gap is in storytelling, global marketing, and distribution systems, all relatively easier to build.

item.title: Half of Clay's customers simply use Claude Code instead of Clay's own agent
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-latentspace-clay-的客户里-一半人干脆用-claude-code-而不是-clay-自家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-latentspace-clay-的客户里-一半人干脆用-claude-code-而不是-clay-自家/
item.description: This AI agent company for sales teams is explicit: it does not want its own agent to outperform using Clay plus Claude Code, because it wants to be underlying infrastructure for go-to-market, not another gatekeeping chat interface.
item.content:encoded:
This AI agent company for sales teams is explicit: it does not want its own agent to outperform using Clay plus Claude Code, because it wants to be underlying infrastructure for go-to-market, not another gatekeeping chat interface.

Engineering details and architectural decisions can be directly adapted to other projects, but the content leans toward engineering leads building vertical agents; general readers can jump to the second half.

3:15 Go-to-market engineers represent a shift from hiring more salespeople to building systems
Jeff Barg explains the term's origin. In the 2010s, companies grew sales by hiring more salespeople and marketers. With LLMs, agents can now crawl the web, score customers, and execute decisions—so a new type of person emerged: someone who uses software engineering methods for growth, writing prompts, doing data engineering, building automation systems. This role combines agent engineering, data engineering, and traditional software engineering. It previously lived scattered across revenue operations without a distinct identity.

25:34 Without CRM data, agents cannot function as sales representatives
The first version of Sculptor's biggest limitation wasn't model capability but context. The agent couldn't access CRM data or see the actual results after an outbound email was sent, so it couldn't make judgments like a real sales rep. The team rebuilt the entire platform's data layer (Audiences), aligning first-party data from CRMs, Gong call recordings, and Clay's own company dataset into a single source of truth for customers and contacts—now the agent has something to work with.

29:45 Post-training becomes cost-effective above roughly ten million dollars in inference spending
Jeff said Clay spent the past 18 months thinking in-house model training was unrealistic, only recently reconsidering. He gave an experience threshold: only when inference costs reach roughly $10 million to $100 million does savings become "chunky" enough to justify open-source model fine-tuning or distillation; otherwise most companies arrive too early with insufficient inference volume to make the savings meaningful.

31:47 Scoring 40 million companies costs roughly fifteen hundred dollars in total
Clay's company dataset has 40 million companies; each LinkedIn profile is about 1,000 tokens, plus a customer's ideal customer profile (ICP) is roughly 500 tokens, so one "is this company right for my product?" judgment requires 1,500 tokens. At $42 per billion tokens, scoring every company in the world costs roughly $1,500. For comparison: qualified leads typically cost $1–$10 each; phone appointments run $10–$100.

34:55 Users hate choosing models, but Clay won't eliminate manual selection
Jeff says directly: "Our users hate the model selector." Most customers dislike having to choose which model—they want to get the job done, not study each new model's eval scores. Clay is launching "auto mode," handing model selection back to the system, since task-level routing (finding Apple's CEO versus a rare startup's CEO need very different model capability) is more rational than manual choice. But he concedes this requires customers to "trust that we spend your tokens well"—a trust mechanism, not a transparency one.

41:17 Production-grade agent experience remains nearly unavailable in the job market
The hardest hire for Clay is someone with real production-agent engineering experience. This scarcity is steeper in New York than the Bay Area. The reason is straightforward: ChatGPT is only four years old; the pool of people with one-plus years building production agents is small to begin with, further narrowing the hiring range beyond just geography.

48:29 Clay deliberately avoids making its own agent better than using Clay plus Claude Code
Clay built a CLI and agent sandbox, nearly matching all capabilities of external coding agents, but Jeff is explicit: "We deliberately do not want our agent to be obviously better than directly using Clay plus Claude Code." The team measured usage of their own harness versus external ones (mainly Claude Code) and found nearly 50/50 split, more balanced than expected. Clay's positioning is to become "agent infrastructure for the go-to-market space," not to seize the entry point—why it invests across CLI, MCP, and API forms.

55:50 OpenAI cancelled partnership days before launch, then reversed the decision
Clay was an early commercial partner for ChatGPT apps, so it pulled a quarter of engineering for a month-long sprint. Two days before launch, OpenAI notified them of an indefinite delay. Clay judged the bet itself still sound and chose to keep developing on schedule. Three to four days later, OpenAI reversed course and resumed the partnership. Jeff uses this to illustrate "institutional courage": in a fast-moving moment, decisions reverse often; teams cannot abandon bets just because one rejection arrives.

item.title: Riemann Hypothesis proved—but the proof is unreadable to humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-fromfirstprinc-黎曼猜想被证明-但证明本身人类读不懂/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-fromfirstprinc-黎曼猜想被证明-但证明本身人类读不懂/
item.description: This proof is not a traditional paper, but a collection of files written in Lean code that even the author hasn't necessarily fully read through. The mathematics community is both amazed and in heated debate over whether AI mathematical proofs count as ‘understanding’.
item.content:encoded:
This proof is not a traditional paper, but a collection of files written in Lean code that even the author hasn't necessarily fully read through. The mathematics community is both amazed and in heated debate over whether AI mathematical proofs count as ‘understanding’.

This episode has extremely high information density, covering the two-hundred-year history of the Riemann Hypothesis through the mechanism of the proof and insider details of the AI mathematics arms race; we recommend listening to it in full.

2:38 Three major mathematical breakthroughs in six months represent a historical watershed
The opening establishes that over the past half year, the mathematics community has experienced three major breakthroughs: the Jacobi Conjecture disproven by AI in July, the Navier-Stokes equations attacked, and the Riemann Hypothesis proved last week. The host places this pace alongside the James Webb Space Telescope's transformation of astronomy and CRISPR's transformation of biology, calling it a true dividing line in the history of science—and one that has now happened more than once in mathematics within just months.

13:54 Euler's algebraic sieving permanently bound primes to the zeta function
Krishna reconstructs how Euler transformed the zeta function—the sum of reciprocals of integers—into an infinite product over all primes. Each time you multiply by ‘1 − 1/p^s’, it is equivalent to sieving out multiples of 2, 3, 5 in turn until only primes remain. The derivation itself is heuristic, not rigorous, but it was the first to weld primes and the zeta function together—the true starting point for more than two centuries of research that followed.

1:12:50 All nontrivial zeros must have equal influence on prime distribution
If some nontrivial zero of the zeta function had real part not equal to one-half—say, three-quarters—its amplitude would dwarf all others and overwhelm the rest in a sufficiently large range, causing prime distribution to show long gaps followed by sudden clustering, rather than the near-random distribution we see today. The Riemann Hypothesis amounts to saying that every nontrivial zero contributes equally to prime randomness; no single zero can dominate the trend.

1:26:40 Every new model is tested on the Riemann Hypothesis as a secret competition
On August 11, Alpöge let an internal model attempt a neighboring problem: the proportion of nontrivial zeros on the critical line. Humans had previously pushed this to 41.6%; Claude pushed it to two-thirds on the spot. The host notes that cutting-edge labs test each new model on the Riemann Hypothesis first—this is never accidental but a tacit competition between two companies.

1:30:45 OpenAI's 700 papers were published before collaborators could announce their own work
On October 6, OpenAI published 700 mathematical preprints online, including a quasi-Riemann Hypothesis result narrowing the range of nontrivial zeros to exclude the interval (7/8, 1)—enough for a Fields Medal in a mathematician under forty. But the mathematics community erupted, because this release front-ran the collaborative progress that Alpöge and other mathematicians were making. Alpöge himself became fixated, suspecting a mole between the two companies, and from that day forward committed fully to the Riemann Hypothesis.

1:42:00 Using primes to constrain zeros instead of vice versa broke the circular logic
Conventionally, one uses zeta zeros to calculate prime distribution; this proof reverses it. First, it uses Chebyshev-style combinatorial tricks—for example, the binomial coefficient C(20,10), where dividing numerator by denominator leaves only primes between 10 and 20—to independently bound the error in prime counting without relying on the zeta function. Then it backsolves from that bound to constrain where nontrivial zeros must fall, thereby avoiding circular reasoning.

1:46:30 Formal proofs that only machines can verify still count as proofs
Alpöge's proof is not a traditional paper but a collection of Lean files that even he admits he cannot fully read. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad publicly criticized it; University of Chicago's Frank Caligari countered with an analogy to Borges's Library of Babel: Alpöge merely found the book on the shelf that contains the proof, and now everyone can try to read it together. The two camps have not converged, and Conrad happens to be the doctoral advisor of the scholar who spent twelve years on a hand-written proof.

1:51:16 P versus NP is likely next, and solving it could break digital encryption
The episode ends by noting that rumors of P versus NP solutions are circulating on Twitter; if solved, the impact extends beyond mathematics to the entire digital economy that relies on cryptography. According to rumors, relevant parties will brief governments and banks first. The host says that if the brightest minds in mathematics haven't yet worked out how humanity should live with this kind of AI capability, the question will soon spread to physics and beyond.

item.title: The brain's forebrain and hindbrain originate from two distinct cell types, not one
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-fromourneurons-大脑其实来自两种祖细胞-前脑与后脑从胚胎期就分道扬镳/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-fromourneurons-大脑其实来自两种祖细胞-前脑与后脑从胚胎期就分道扬镳/
item.description: A Stanford team discovered that forebrain and hindbrain are determined not by a single type of early progenitor cell, but by two fate-restricted progenitor cell types that exist simultaneously in the embryo. This overturns the classical model, in place since 1952, that a single progenitor cell generates the entire brain.
item.content:encoded:
A Stanford team discovered that forebrain and hindbrain are determined not by a single type of early progenitor cell, but by two fate-restricted progenitor cell types that exist simultaneously in the embryo. This overturns the classical model, in place since 1952, that a single progenitor cell generates the entire brain.

Best for those interested in developmental biology and mechanisms of neurodegenerative disease. The information density isn't peak, but there are several specific stories and an unexpected finding about Ozempic worth listening to in particular.

3:04 The 1952 classical model claimed the brain has a single origin
The renowned embryologist Pieter Nieuwkoop proposed in 1952 that the entire brain originates from a single class of progenitor cells called the neural ectoderm—a claim that has since become textbook consensus. When Kyle Loh's team went back to find this cell type, however, they discovered not one, but two progenitor cell types existing simultaneously, which became the starting point for their research.

5:40 The key difference lies in cell fate commitment, not anatomical location
During embryonic development, there's a stage where a single cell can still generate all organs throughout the body. At some point thereafter, this cell loses the ability to form skin and intestines, becoming capable only of forming the brain—this is called the first-generation brain progenitor. The real question is: at that moment, can this initial brain progenitor still generate the entire brain, or has it already been split into two separate paths—one leading to forebrain and one to hindbrain? The team set out to verify whether this fate commitment had already occurred.

6:58 A headless chicken that lived 1.5 years shows the hindbrain runs vital functions
In 1945, a farmer severed a chicken's head but cut incompletely, removing the forebrain and midbrain while leaving the hindbrain intact. The chicken, named Mike, survived for 1.5 years. Kyle Loh uses this story to illustrate that it is the hindbrain/brainstem, not the forebrain (which we typically associate with cognition and memory), that keeps us alert, breathing, and maintains our heartbeat.

8:56 Behind this research is a patient: a child with type 1 SMA
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is the leading genetic cause of death in infants under one year old. One of Kyle Loh's colleagues has a child diagnosed with type 1 SMA and receiving treatment at Stanford Hospital. The hindbrain motor neurons control facial, jaw, eye, tongue, and neck muscles; when these neurons are damaged, the child cannot eat or swallow, and food entering the airway can be fatal. This direct motivation drove the team's persistence in generating hindbrain neurons in culture.

16:07 The dual-origin pattern traces back to acorn worms from over 500 million years ago
In collaboration with Stanford evolutionary biologist Chris Lowe, the team discovered that the same dual brain progenitor cell structure exists across humans, mice, chickens, zebrafish, and acorn worms—organisms that diverged from humans over 500 million years ago. This demonstrates that the dual-origin pattern is a conserved evolutionary feature across species, not a human-specific coincidence.

17:23 Jellyfish's paired nerve rings suggest the brain is fundamentally an assembled organ
This material was too speculative to include in the paper but appears only in the podcast: cnidarians like jellyfish have no single brain; instead, they have a physically separate nerve ring at each end of their body. Kyle Loh speculates that the notion of 'the brain as an organ' may be a historical bias stemming from scientists first studying humans and mice, which have a single brain enclosed in a skull. Had they first studied jellyfish, the conclusion might have been entirely different.

21:38 No animal exists with only a hindbrain and no forebrain, undermining textbook claims
Textbooks claim the hindbrain is 'evolutionarily the oldest component' because animals had to learn to move before becoming intelligent. But Kyle Loh points out that if the hindbrain were truly older, we should find existing animals with only a hindbrain and no forebrain. To his knowledge, no such animal exists, making the claim that 'the hindbrain is more primitive' questionable.

26:02 Ozempic suppresses appetite through the hindbrain, not the hypothalamus, a 2024 study showed
Textbooks hold that the hypothalamus in the forebrain controls hunger and body weight. However, a 2024 Nature paper found that in mice given Ozempic, destroying neurons expressing the GLP-1 receptor in the hypothalamus had minimal effect on the drug's efficacy; destroying hindbrain neurons expressing this receptor, by contrast, nearly eliminated weight loss from Ozempic. This suggests the true site of action for Ozempic is an evolutionarily ancient hunger circuit in the hindbrain, explaining why years of drug development targeting the hypothalamus has yielded limited results.

item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated 11 days after removal: market power overrides national security
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-cogrev-黄仁勋被罢免11天后复职-市场权力压倒国家安全考量/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-cogrev-黄仁勋被罢免11天后复职-市场权力压倒国家安全考量/
item.description: After Nvidia's board briefly removed Jensen Huang, stock declines forced the company to reinstate him within 11 days, proving that ‘number must go up’market pressure overrides corporate governance and even national security.
item.content:encoded:
After Nvidia's board briefly removed Jensen Huang, stock declines forced the company to reinstate him within 11 days, proving that ‘number must go up’market pressure overrides corporate governance and even national security.

The first half is heated debate over Christiano's 10% AI-risk thesis; the second half is hard analysis of Nvidia's competitive moats and Taiwan chip geopolitics, densely packed with information and presenting conflicting arguments across both sections.

0:00 Paul Christiano now estimates 10% annual AI takeover risk
In recent interviews, Christiano told hosts he estimates the risk of AI takeover next year at ‘more like a 10% risk than a 1% risk’, with ‘maybe a 1/3 chance that we have superintelligence within one year’ if development doesn't slow. These figures, far higher than the previously assumed ~1% risk, compress the timeline from decades to months. This estimate anchored the episode's core debate, with other guests responding throughout.

0:52 What fails control is the market system, not AI models
Prakash Narayanan reframes AI safety: rather than asking whether a model might escape control, ask whether the market-driven economic system will. ‘The superintelligence is actually the market. It's not the thing inside the chat box.’ History's deepest changes stem not from machines acting directly but from market incentives driving human behavior. This redefines the core disagreement across the episode, demonstrated later when market pressure forces Huang's reinstatement.

23:57 Unconditional cash transfers cut infant mortality nearly in half
GiveDirectly's decade-long study tracking over 100,000 births found that in communities receiving cash transfers, ‘infant and child mortality was forty eight percent lower’. Nick Allardice explains the mechanism: mothers with resources leave work earlier, secure better nutrition, and access healthcare more frequently and earlier. This was among the episode's rare empirical data points, disconnected from the AI debate.

37:21 Market and government have already surrendered control
Prakash argues that loss of control pervades existing systems: governments ceded price-setting to markets; airline and telecom deregulation exemplify the pattern. These aren't fruits of benevolence but stable equilibria reached through competition, generating both growth and mutual gain. He uses this to challenge the assumption that AI loss of control would be unprecedented, suggesting multi-agent systems will ultimately self-organize under market pressure—though other guests did not fully endorse this.

1:10:27 Long-skeptical AI researchers now believe in intelligence explosion
Tom Davidson from Forethought has long doubted AI explosion theories, but recent events shifted his view: Hugging Face multi-agent experiments, mathematical breakthroughs, Anthropic's doubled research velocity. He concedes bottleneck arguments sound coherent but ‘it just doesn't look right’ because last year's results massively exceeded skeptics' predictions. His change of mind matters more than the conclusion itself: a measured researcher publicly admitting misjudgment.

1:29:04 Huang's personal relationships, not CUDA, are Nvidia's real moat
Prakash argues that CUDA alone doesn't account for Nvidia's competitive advantage. The genuine edge is Huang's ability to make credible multi-year promises to suppliers years in advance—in East Asian business culture, local suppliers trust personal relationships over legal contracts. Without Huang, coordination requires intermediaries, adding communication delays and working capital costs that would push gross margins from 72% to 50%, eroding roughly $1 trillion in market value. This recasts Nvidia's valuation from technology moat to one person's personal credit.

1:33:37 When stock prices fall, national security yields to economic growth
Huang's forced reinstatement reflects core logic: stock declines make economic growth desire overcome security considerations, including national security. Nathan Labenz observes ‘the market in the West is the highest authority’—Americans care about growth, low inflation, and low unemployment, not legal process. Prakash highlights a paradox: if removing Huang violated governance procedures, his reinstatement cannot be ‘unfair’, suggesting American systems are evolving toward rule by the highest power holder's personal will.

1:51:59 Demanding AI comprehension would have frozen progress at GPT-2
When others proposed ‘comprehension audits’ requiring third parties to verify that employees can explain each capability improvement, Prakash countered with a hard constraint: most AI researchers barely understand neural networks themselves; capabilities advance far faster than understanding. Requiring full explanation before each step would stall progress at roughly GPT-2 level, six years ago. This differs from pharma, where human trials enable gradual understanding—AI capability growth simply outpaces explanation.

item.title: Diabetics receiving healthy food see medical costs cut by two-thirds
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-a16z-糖尿病患者获得健康食物后-医疗支出直接砍掉三分之二/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-a16z-糖尿病患者获得健康食物后-医疗支出直接砍掉三分之二/
item.description: Food insecurity correlates with medical spending rises: mild +15%, moderate +30%, severe up to +70%—yet providing healthy food costs far less than medication.
item.content:encoded:
Food insecurity correlates with medical spending rises: mild +15%, moderate +30%, severe up to +70%—yet providing healthy food costs far less than medication.

An older interview on food-as-medicine with solid underlying data and examples, but the discussion stays conceptual and advocacy-driven—no specific companies or products—so skim for key insights and quotes.

1:05 Food's compliance advantage over drugs: eating happens whether prescribed or not
Josh Hicks points out that unlike other medical interventions, food is a consumer good everyone eats multiple times daily regardless of health benefit. When customers simply subscribed to his meal delivery service, many became healthier ‘almost by accident.’ Food interventions have an inherent compliance advantage because eating requires no additional persuasion.

2:48 Changing checkout screens beats persuading people to diet
Meal delivery and online shopping turn food choices into manipulable data, with each person living in their own food media bubble. Hicks argues that modifying what appears on the digital checkout page for the most vulnerable and sick—hiding candy bars, for instance—works better than dietary persuasion alone. Academic evidence and real cases support the approach.

4:09 Integration means WIC and SNAP users can buy prescribed food directly
Andrea Feinberg identifies the real barrier as payment system integration, not technology. WIC and SNAP beneficiaries need to purchase recommended healthy foods using those benefits—this system must connect. She notes that metabolic dysfunction and malnutrition made populations more fragile during COVID, problems often rooted in food insecurity or poor eating choices. While not easy, the solution is relatively straightforward.

5:14 Each tier of food insecurity triggers a step-up in medical costs
Feinberg cites concrete data: mild food insecurity correlates with roughly 15% higher annual medical spending, moderate with 30%, severe with 70% or more. With U.S. annual medical spending at $3.5 trillion, much of it stems from unmet social needs. Healthcare investment flows toward social determinants only when the system is rewarded for keeping people healthy.

10:28 Diabetics on food support see medical costs plummet two-thirds
Feinberg shares results from a Geisinger project: patients with uncontrolled diabetes who received healthy food, education, and social support showed marked improvement in HbA1c (blood sugar control) and total medical cost decline of 60% or more—with the most severe cases dropping by two-thirds. She notes that diabetes medications can cost hundreds of dollars monthly while providing food to someone food-insecure costs roughly $50 monthly.

11:29 Doctors train one hour on nutrition, leaving medicine unprepared for food
Feinberg cites often-quoted data: standard medical degrees include only about one hour of nutrition education, partly why food-as-medicine hasn't integrated into healthcare. Her generation of doctors received almost no real nutrition training; now medical schools are adding cooking programs and food-as-medicine courses. Patients are more willing to try an approach only if their doctors believe in it—why Geisinger requires clinicians to prescribe medically tailored meals formally, like drugs.

15:31 Infrastructure beats behavior: fluoridation works without asking anyone to change
Julie Yu draws a parallel: adding fluoride to municipal water prevented millions of children's cavities annually with zero behavioral change required. She asks whether medical interventions like statins could one day embed in public infrastructure, eliminating the need for payment and behavior modification. Feinberg responds that fluoridation itself isn't universal—she's seen rural Pennsylvania communities still lacking it, with dental consequences. She argues healthy food should be a ‘basic guarantee’ for every child, adult, and senior, and doesn't see it as a distant fantasy.

item.title: Traditional CAPE Valuation Is Miscalculated: The Market Isn't As Expensive As It Looks
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-rationalreminder-传统cape估值被算错了-市场没有看起来那么贵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-rationalreminder-传统cape估值被算错了-市场没有看起来那么贵/
item.description: Traditional CAPE weights components by earnings rather than market value, underweighting high-priced, low-earnings tech stocks; using market-value-weighted component CAPE instead shows the US market's current overvaluation as less severe than official CAPE suggests, and predictive accuracy improves by 20–25%.
item.content:encoded:
Traditional CAPE weights components by earnings rather than market value, underweighting high-priced, low-earnings tech stocks; using market-value-weighted component CAPE instead shows the US market's current overvaluation as less severe than official CAPE suggests, and predictive accuracy improves by 20–25%.

Worth hearing if you want to understand what the current 40x CAPE actually means and whether this widely-used metric has calculation flaws; the second half, focused on the permanent portfolio, has lower information density but still contains useful insights.

2:04 Ten-year expected returns depend on current valuations, not historical averages
Ben Marshall notes that for forecasting 100-year returns, using the historical 10% annual average over the past 100 years is a reasonable starting point; but most people care about the next 10 years, where historical averages fall short because research shows ten-year expected returns are conditional on current valuations: high valuations imply low expected returns, and vice versa. Ben Felix adds that US historical returns also cannot represent global expectations, since American actual performance has significantly exceeded other markets.

11:12 The three-factor model is about 30% more accurate than naive forecasting
Marshall's team tested four combinations—dividends alone, dividends plus growth, valuation alone, and dividends plus growth plus valuation—and found that the three-factor model using CAPE as the valuation input was most consistent. By out-of-sample R-squared and mean absolute error, it outperformed naive forecasts (assuming the future equals the historical average) by about 30%. While not perfect, this improvement is substantial compared to other published forecasting models.

13:08 Current CAPE approaches 40, more than double the historical average
As of the recording date (November 26), Shiller CAPE stands at approximately 40–41, versus a historical average of around 18, meaning current valuations far exceed historical levels. The three-factor model also incorporates dividend yield (currently at historic lows) and earnings growth assumptions. Marshall believes the market's current pricing reflects very robust expectations for future earnings growth, whether this materializes remains to be seen.

14:34 Ten-year investors should reduce stock allocations; thirty- to forty-year investors can ignore valuations
The model is valid only for ten-year forecasts and offers no predictive value for next month, next year, or even the next three years. For ten-year investors, high valuations may require reducing stock allocations; for thirty- to forty-year investors, they can ignore current overvaluation because a long enough holding period dilutes near-term valuation effects. Ben Felix notes that PWL uses a weighted expected return estimate combining 25% of the CAPE reciprocal with 75% of the historical average.

19:25 CAPE's fatal flaw: using earnings-weighted ratios to forecast a market-value-weighted index
Traditional CAPE has two overlooked mismatches. First, the index's current constituents' prices are compared against ten years ago's entirely different constituents' reported historical earnings—for example, Tesla replaced Apartment Investment in the S&P 500 in December 2020, so when calculating 2021 CAPE, the numerator included Tesla's price but the denominator mixed in the real estate company's historical earnings. Second, more counterintuitively, traditional CAPE weights by earnings scale, not market value, meaning an earnings-weighted ratio forecasts a market-value-weighted index return, introducing inherent bias. Research also found this problem affects only ratios where the denominator is not price or market value (like CAPE), not metrics like dividend yield or price-to-book, where the denominator is already price-based.

24:53 Reweighting each stock's CAPE by market value boosts predictive power by 20–25%
The solution is to calculate CAPE for each stock individually, then aggregate using market-value weights rather than earnings weights to obtain component CAPE, aligning the weighting method perfectly with the S&P 500's own market-value-weighted approach. By out-of-sample R-squared, this change boosts predictive accuracy by 20–25%; measured by certainty equivalent return, the economic value for asset allocation also shows investors genuinely benefit. In 1999, when tech valuations soared, traditional CAPE's earnings weighting suppressed high-price, low-earnings tech weights, while component CAPE assigned them far greater weight—the gap was especially pronounced in that period.

36:40 Both versions identify overvaluation, but traditional and component CAPE score it differently
Currently traditional CAPE is about 1.8 times the historical average (80% above), while component CAPE is about 1.6 times (60% above)—both signal overvaluation, but component CAPE's degree is notably more modest. Marshall sees this as one reason component CAPE has forecasted better recently: valuations stayed high over the past decade, but the market performed well overall, making traditional CAPE appear too pessimistic, while component CAPE's optimistic bias actually tracked reality more closely.

45:37 The permanent portfolio's historical outperformance was largely underwritten by gold price appreciation
Marshall acknowledges his paper did not conduct deep analysis but speculates that Harry Browne's permanent portfolio (25% each in stocks, bonds, gold, and cash) outperformed traditional stock-bond portfolios from 1972 to 1991 largely due to gold's extraordinary performance during that period (after the US left the gold standard and Americans regained the freedom to own gold), rather than inherent superiority of the portfolio structure itself—since relative to traditional portfolios, the permanent portfolio's main distinction is gold overweight. Ben Felix later adds he ran out-of-sample tests from 2012 onward to verify this.

item.title: UPS won not through technology but by consolidating scattered wagons into a unified network
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-oddlots-ups-不是靠技术发家的-它赢在把分散的马车整合成一张网/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-oddlots-ups-不是靠技术发家的-它赢在把分散的马车整合成一张网/
item.description: What gave early UPS the edge over rivals was not trucks or barcodes, but a deceptively simple organizational innovation: consolidating shipments at a central sorting hub before distributing them — far more efficient than route-by-route direct delivery.
item.content:encoded:
What gave early UPS the edge over rivals was not trucks or barcodes, but a deceptively simple organizational innovation: consolidating shipments at a central sorting hub before distributing them — far more efficient than route-by-route direct delivery.

An episode that explains how a century-old private logistics giant built itself on organizational innovation rather than technical leadership — for anyone interested in business history, logistics, and how monopolies form; information density is moderately high.

10:18 UPS started as a Seattle messenger company, not from nationwide ambitions
When Casey founded UPS in 1907, it was a messenger business — delivering dinners, luggage, store packages by bicycle and streetcar. Customers found the company through word-of-mouth phone referrals. Seattle even had two incompatible telephone systems; UPS had to maintain two lines to reach all customers. For its first 12 years, the company operated only in Seattle and had no grand ambitions to expand nationally.

11:19 The centralized sorting hub, not trucks or technology, was UPS's moat
Casey's breakthrough was not technical but organizational. He transformed the one-to-one messenger model into a hub-and-spoke system: collect all packages at a central sorting station, mix them together, then distribute them to drivers by route. This meant one truck could carry shipments for ten stores instead of each store sending its own truck down the same street. The idea seems obvious in hindsight, but getting retailers to accept that packages would go to a hub first required them to embrace scientific management thinking, which was fashionable at the time.

17:27 World War I draft shortages handed UPS a sudden advantage over retail delivery
During World War I, the U.S. government discovered roughly 200,000 people worked in retail delivery and saw this as wasteful redundancy. It pressed the industry to improve efficiency. At the same time, retailers' wagoners and drivers were drafted or poached by shipyards paying higher wages. Facing labor shortages, retailers couldn't maintain their own delivery operations. This opened the door for UPS, which could deliver the same volume with far fewer people. Suddenly, large numbers of retailers began outsourcing their delivery to UPS.

25:37 Long contracts locked in customers more than efficiency did
UPS required retailers to sign contracts stipulating exact times when packages had to be ready. Drivers would not wait if packages weren't prepared on time — the whole route schedule took priority. These rigid terms, unprecedented in the industry, combined with contracts typically lasting five years or more, gave UPS confidence to invest in sorting hubs. For retailers, once they sold their stables and fleets, returning to self-delivery became extremely difficult. The result was near-total absence of competition in markets where UPS operated.

32:56 UPS lobbied regulators to limit itself to small packages only
When UPS acquired a Southern California trucking company with a common carrier license — permitting it to haul any cargo — Casey did something unexpected: he asked regulators to restrict UPS to small packages only. His reasoning was that only single-person-deliverable items achieved true efficiency. This reversed the typical industry strategy of expanding scope, but regulators agreed that package delivery was fundamentally different from general freight. In return, UPS received special permission to deviate from assigned routes and deliver directly to residential addresses.

38:00 Internal promotion culture left UPS without technical talent when tech arrived
Casey believed in promoting from within. Good drivers became supervisors, supervisors became managers. This built organizational loyalty but created a critical blind spot: the company had almost no computer scientists or technologists. When FedEx and other new entrants arrived with barcodes and advanced technology, UPS fell behind. Tech talent also avoided joining what was perceived as a ‘truck company.’ UPS was forced to hire externally and catch up.

42:09 UPS's unified management culture became a liability in international expansion
UPS attempted to transplant its rigidly hierarchical ‘UPS way’ — with policies dictating every operational detail — directly into acquired German operations. The result was a disaster. Management practices routine in America struck German workers and managers as bizarre and unacceptable. The company was forced to pause and rethink, ultimately adapting its approach to local conditions. It learned that UPS's tightly unified corporate culture itself could become an obstacle to global expansion.

item.title: The widowed magazine editor who pushed Thanksgiving to become a national holiday
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-throughline-感恩节国定假日的推手-是一位丈夫早逝的杂志女编辑/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-throughline-感恩节国定假日的推手-是一位丈夫早逝的杂志女编辑/
item.description: Over three decades, Sarah Josepha Hale lobbied governors, congressmen, and presidents by letter, hoping a nationwide Thanksgiving would prevent civil war. The holiday took hold, but after her death, her narrative of unity was replaced by a different myth: Native American and Puritan friendship.
item.content:encoded:
Over three decades, Sarah Josepha Hale lobbied governors, congressmen, and presidents by letter, hoping a nationwide Thanksgiving would prevent civil war. The holiday took hold, but after her death, her narrative of unity was replaced by a different myth: Native American and Puritan friendship.

Learn how the 'first Thanksgiving' legend was constructed and how it diverges from the actual history of ethnic violence. This episode traces two parallel stories—the holiday's political origins and the myth's formation—with clarity that rewards close attention.

3:11 The 1621 meal was set in extreme power imbalance
The episode recounts the 1621 gathering between English colonists and the Wampanoag people, emphasizing that it was no simple friendship story. The English were few and struggling to survive; the Wampanoag outnumbered them at least twenty to one and held real power in the encounter. Historian David Silverman stresses that reducing this meeting to a story of 'gratitude' strips it from its actual historical context.

4:20 Fifty years later, friendship turned to war
In 1675, Wampanoag chief Metacom appealed to Rhode Island's attorney general, recounting how his father had given land to the English and taught them farming and fishing. Now, the English had reversed positions but no longer respected the Wampanoag, prompting war. The conflict lasted nearly three years; the English won. Thousands of Wampanoag were killed or enslaved to the Caribbean and Mediterranean. Metacom was beheaded, his head displayed for twenty years at Plymouth Colony—the same place where the 1621 meal occurred.

13:44 She raised five children alone by writing after her husband's sudden death
Sarah married lawyer David Hale at twenty-five. After eight years of happy marriage, he died suddenly, leaving her with four children and one on the way, nearly destitute. Convention dictated that a widow without a husband should place her children with relatives, but she refused. Instead, she earned her living writing poetry, essays, and novels. Her anti-slavery novel Northwood established her reputation in Boston intellectual circles and led to an invitation to edit a women's magazine.

20:04 She saw Thanksgiving as a tool to build one American culture
Sarah believed the American Revolution had unified the colonies politically, but not culturally. She hoped that all Americans celebrating Thanksgiving on the same day would foster a sense of belonging to 'one big family.' She publicly declared that if Thanksgiving became fixed, it would become a force promoting the 'national spirit' that could prevent civil war—transforming the holiday from a family gathering into a political project.

30:24 Southern leaders saw Thanksgiving as a Trojan horse for abolition
In 1856, Virginia Governor Henry Wise replied to Sarah, calling Thanksgiving a 'damned Yankee holiday' because Northern ministers had turned Thanksgiving sermons into abolitionist propaganda. The episode suggests Wise's judgment wasn't entirely wrong—the anti-slavery movement was indeed intertwined with New England religious life at the time. Virginia did not celebrate Thanksgiving that year.

33:34 Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday five days after Gettysburg
In 1863, following the Battle of Gettysburg, Sarah wrote to Lincoln again. This time, Lincoln responded within five days, issuing a proclamation that made Thanksgiving a national holiday, calling on all Americans to celebrate ‘with one heart and one voice.’ Sarah's decades of lobbying had finally borne fruit—but the holiday was established not as a simple harvest celebration, but as a tool for wartime national unity.

41:02 The 'first Thanksgiving' legend began with a footnote
In 1836, when William Apes publicly critiqued colonial history, he never mentioned Thanksgiving—because most Americans hadn't yet imagined Native Americans and Puritans sharing a meal. That vision came later: in the 1840s, a New England minister publishing original documents added a footnote stating ‘this was the first Thanksgiving.’ The legend grew from that single footnote. But it only truly took hold in American society after Lincoln's 1863 proclamation.

44:05 A 1912 painting embedded civilization versus savagery into American textbooks
Painter Jean-Leon Jerome Ferris completed an oil painting titled ‘The First Thanksgiving’ in 1912. White colonists sit at the table while Native Americans sit on the ground, dressed in artist-imagined feathers and beads. Historian David Silverman points out that this composition was deliberately designed to reinforce an 'English civilization versus Native American savagery' binary—a framework that had shaped white Americans' understanding of themselves and Native peoples for four centuries. By the early twentieth century, this became the standard template for school Thanksgiving pageants.

item.title: He kept the republic's shell for fourteen hundred years, but had already drained its power
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-ancients-他把共和国的躯壳留下一千四百年-权力却早已被掏空/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-ancients-他把共和国的躯壳留下一千四百年-权力却早已被掏空/
item.description: Augustus never formally abolished republican institutions—the consul, Senate, and tribune titles remained—he simply extracted the real authority behind these positions one piece at a time and consolidated it all to himself.
item.content:encoded:
Augustus never formally abolished republican institutions—the consul, Senate, and tribune titles remained—he simply extracted the real authority behind these positions one piece at a time and consolidated it all to himself.

For anyone wanting to understand how power can be completely restructured without changing a system's appearance; the narrative runs from Octavian taking arms at nineteen through Augustus on his deathbed on the Palatine Hill, covering nearly sixty years of his complete political web of intrigue.

6:08 Claiming ‘vengeance for his father’ silenced every opponent
At twenty, Octavian brought armed troops toward Rome. He didn't claim he wanted to seize power—he claimed he was avenging Caesar, who had been assassinated. In Roman culture, no one could argue against this. The Senate found itself trapped by its own moral logic and couldn't stop him from taking power. This became a strategy he would repeat throughout his life: always wrapping his power grabs in an unassailable justification.

8:12 He dismantled the republic while keeping it alive for another thousand years
Augustus didn't abolish the consulship, tribunate, or other republican offices. Instead, he carefully extracted the real authority behind these positions one piece at a time and gathered it all to himself, while the empty titles persisted. The result: Roman institutions looked the same for more than a thousand years, but had become a monarchy in substance, so much so that he himself could believe—and declare—that he had ‘restored the republic’.

17:30 ‘Handing back power’, he kept the three most garrisoned provinces
In 27 BCE, Augustus announced he was returning control of all provinces. But he kept three: Gaul, Egypt, and Syria—precisely where Rome's legions were concentrated. He framed this as an act of selflessness, as if it barely mattered. In fact, he had secured complete control of all military forces.

36:06 He bought the entire Senate with favors and debts
Entry to the Senate required a certain wealth threshold. Augustus raised it, then ‘loaned’ or even gave money to candidates who couldn't meet it. He handed out endorsements and his daughter's dowry with equal generosity. Each recipient's price was their vote in every future Senate decision. By 23 BCE, so many people owed him favors or money that any opposition couldn't coalesce.

41:19 Tribune's power and supreme command were what ‘emperor’ truly meant
The 23 BCE settlement gave him two things: supreme command over all armies and lifelong tribunician power—which made his person sacred and gave him veto power over the Senate. These two authorities didn't depend on any republican office. Every future Roman emperor would inherit these same two powers.

55:08 His adultery law ultimately punished his own daughter
Augustus passed laws strictly punishing adultery. Years later, his daughter Julia's private life was exposed as chaotic, with one lover being the son of his former enemy Mark Antony. He raged and exiled her to an island, forbidding her from ever being near another man, and told those around him he wished she were dead. He made no exception for his daughter. It made his moral legislation seem uncompromising and closed off any ‘do as I say, not as I do’ criticism.

1:03:35 Three legions were annihilated, yet he emerged completely unscathed
Three Roman legions were wiped out in the forest of Teutoburg—lost by Varus, Augustus's handpicked aide. It should have been a catastrophe, enough to shake his rule. Instead, Augustus staged a spectacular show of grief: weeping, refusing to shave. No one called him to account for his poor judgment. By then his authority was so secure that even defeat couldn't hurt him personally.

1:05:41 The power structure he built outlived him by fourteen hundred years
Augustus died peacefully at eighty-six, never overthrown by coup. His successor Tiberius took power smoothly—perhaps the most successful outcome of all his decades of scheming. After his death he was deified, and the system of emperorship he created lasted roughly until 1400 CE—far longer than his own lifetime.

item.title: Three hundred corpses a year: how grave robbers built modern British medicine
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-historyhit-盗尸人一年提供三百具尸体-撑起了英国现代医学的根基/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-historyhit-盗尸人一年提供三百具尸体-撑起了英国现代医学的根基/
item.description: Nineteenth-century English law confined dissection to executed murderers, while medical schools trained thousands of students. Professional body snatchers filled the shortage, supplying over three hundred fresh corpses annually to hospitals.
item.content:encoded:
Nineteenth-century English law confined dissection to executed murderers, while medical schools trained thousands of students. Professional body snatchers filled the shortage, supplying over three hundred fresh corpses annually to hospitals.

An obscure historical corner with granular detail—grave-digging procedures, price lists, court cases—though an advertising segment repeats mid-episode and can be skipped.

5:11 Four executed criminals per year: Henry VIII set dissection's quota
In 1540, Henry VIII merged surgeons and barbers into a single guild and permitted them to dissect four executed felons annually as compensation. This decree permanently bound ‘being dissected’to ‘being criminal’: law-abiding people would not be dissected, only villains deserved it. This notion persisted through 1752's Murder Act, when dissection formally became an added punishment for murderers.

8:23 Medical schools trained thousands of students but legally could dissect twelve corpses annually
Britain then had roughly eight hundred to one thousand medical students, yet only about twelve people were executed annually for murder. Each student needed at least two or three corpses for practice. The supply-demand ratio was absurdly skewed; law had lagged reality for decades, forcing illegal channels to close the gap.

10:28 Anatomists once robbed graves themselves before hiring professional gangs
Before the 1790s, anatomists and students who wanted corpses had to dig them up themselves at night. But when doctors like William Hunter faced hundreds of students, they couldn't personally rob graves constantly. This spawned professional ‘resurrection men’gangs, turning body snatching into a business.

10:38 Stealing the body was legal; stealing the shroud was a crime
English law then didn't recognise the corpse itself as having legal status; possessing a body was only a misdemeanour. But the coffin was property, the burial shroud was property, rings and hairpins were property—damaging the coffin or taking these things constituted theft and criminal damage. Professional body snatchers thus developed a procedure: open only the coffin's top, strip the corpse, leave clothing and jewellery as found, steal only the corpse itself, which ‘counted as’no property.

20:09 One victim's name in the grave robber's sales diary
Professional body snatcher Joseph Naples (约瑟夫·内普尔斯) kept a diary that is essentially a sales ledger; he called the dead ‘things’, anatomists called them ‘subjects’. But in one December 1811 entry, he uniquely wrote a name: Mary Rolph (玛丽·罗尔夫), died December 5. Burial records confirm she was interred that day; Naples' gang dug her up on the 12th—less than a week from burial to theft.

29:27 Burke and Hare never grave-robbed at all
The most famous ‘body snatchers’, Burke and Hare, never actually robbed graves—they murdered tenants and sold them to anatomist Robert Knox. This became known as ‘burking’, smothering via the nose and mouth. The two killed about seventeen people; when exposed, Hare turned against Burke to escape execution, while Burke was hanged and himself became a ‘subject’on the anatomy table.

33:42 The professional grave-robbing leader won price increases by withholding supply
Ben Crouch (本·克劳奇), who monopolised the medical schools' corpse supply, struck when price talks broke down, halting deliveries for roughly four weeks until anatomists agreed to raise rates. This shows that by its late stage, the corpse trade had become a mature business with pricing power and capacity for collective action.

44:59 One attempted corpse sale exposed a murderer and forced legislation
An 1828 parliamentary inquiry should have prompted legislation, but it stalled for years due to controversy over whether to take corpses from the poor. Only in 1831, when John Bishop was caught attempting to sell the corpse of Carlos Ferrari—an Italian boy who sold white mice—was the bill revived and swiftly passed, legalising unclaimed and voluntary-donated corpses for dissection.

item.title: Cook's Death Mystery: Killed as a God or as a Fraud?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-restishistory-库克死亡之谜-他到底是被当神还是被当骗子杀死的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-restishistory-库克死亡之谜-他到底是被当神还是被当骗子杀死的/
item.description: Two anthropologists have debated for decades whether Hawaiians treated Cook as a divine incarnation, with neither convincing the other. What is certain: the collapse of this sacred aura led to him being stabbed to death on the beach.
item.content:encoded:
Two anthropologists have debated for decades whether Hawaiians treated Cook as a divine incarnation, with neither convincing the other. What is certain: the collapse of this sacred aura led to him being stabbed to death on the beach.

For listeners seeking a layered historical mystery: from the cryptic red-robe ritual to the chaos of the final minutes, every detail is crystalline, yet the core question—what Hawaiians actually believed—has no settled answer.

26:46 Cook's Route Matched Lono's Sacred Procession, Making Hawaiians See Him as Divine
When Cook returned to Hawaii, it coincided with Makahiki, the annual harvest festival during which Hawaiians process an idol of the deity Lono (Orono) along the coast, eventually carrying it to the temple at Kealakekua Bay. Anthropologist Marshall Sahlins argues that Cook's sails, shipping route, and landing site entirely mirrored the idol's processional path—sheer coincidence that led Hawaiians to treat him as Lono's incarnation. Cook unknowingly ‘played’ the role: priests anointed him with piglet fat and crowds prostrated before him, all while he stood impassive, allowing the ceremony to proceed.

29:56 Sahlins' Divine Cook Theory Was Attacked as Colonialist Projection, Then Defended
Princeton anthropologist Gananath Obeyesekere fiercely attacks Sahlins' theory, arguing that ‘Orono’ was a term Hawaiians also used for their own kings—so Cook was treated as merely a liminal figure between human and divine, not a true god. Sahlins counters immediately that Obeyesekere is imposing a 20th-century American rational framework onto 18th-century Hawaiian thought, which is itself a form of arrogance. The two reach no consensus even now when interpreting the same historical evidence. The host admits they cannot truly reconstruct how Hawaiians actually thought.

34:59 The King's Grand Parting Gift Was Probably a Ritual to Send the Deity Away
Before Cook departed, King Terriaboo presented him with large quantities of pork, vegetables, and elaborate feather cloaks, with great respect. Crew members later speculated that this grand gift-giving was actually a ritual ‘sending off’ the deity—if Cook was truly a divine incarnation, he should depart after manifesting, not linger. This interpretation proved prophetic: a few days later, storm damage forced Cook's ship to return to Kealakekua Bay, violating the expectation that the god should have already left. This may have prompted a fundamental recalculation among Hawaiians about who Cook truly was.

43:11 Cook's Return to the Bay Shattered the Entire Atmosphere of Reverence
Cook's ship suffered mast damage in a storm and was forced at the last moment to turn back to Kealakekua Bay instead of continuing to Maui to find another anchorage. What greeted them on return was no longer enthusiastic canoes and white cloth, but only a few scattered vessels and a dead-silent coastline. Hawaiians were no longer interested in axes and chisels—they wanted only daggers. Theft became brazen, and attitudes shifted from reverence to mockery and provocation. The host offers one explanation: if Cook was truly treated as a deity, he should not reappear after the festival ended. This ‘return’ itself disrupted the calendrical and ritual balance and might have made people suspect that he was not a god at all but a fraud exposed.

54:30 Cook's Attempt to Seize the King as a Hostage Sparked the Massacre
After a small canoe is stolen, Cook opts for his usual tactic—the method he has used in Tonga and Tahiti—taking King Terriaboo hostage to retrieve the vessel. The operation proceeds smoothly at first; the king even agrees to board the ship. But as they cross the beach, the king's wife rushes forward pleading on her knees while several chiefs restrain him physically. The king sits down on the sand. The crowd swells rapidly to hundreds, possibly thousands. Cook realizes that forcing the king's departure ‘cannot be done without killing people.’ He orders the marines to line up along shore on alert. The situation spins entirely out of control.

57:40 One Officer's Misinterpretation of Cook's Order Left Him Without Escape
In the chaos, Cook waves toward the support boats. Later oil paintings interpret this as Cook ordering the marines to cease fire and demonstrate his humanitarian restraint, but the host suggests this is almost certainly a misreading—Cook was actually signaling the boats to draw closer for evacuation. However, Lieutenant Williamson, commanding the support boats (the same officer who had previously fired without authorization during the initial landing), misunderstands the signal. He interprets Cook's wave as an order to evacuate and withdraws the boats, completely abandoning Cook's group, and even threatens to shoot any subordinate who refuses to obey. This one misunderstanding leaves Cook and his marines with zero naval support.

1:00:55 The Priest's Question Hinted That Hawaiians Might Not Believe Cook Was Dead
After a heavy blow to the head, Cook falls and is stabbed in the neck. He dies in the shallows. Afterward, Hawaiians return his remains piecemeal, wrapped in cloth with black and white feathered cloaks—first a charred piece of thigh, then days later his hands (identified by their distinctive scars), skull, jaw, and feet. Much of his torso never arrives. Most strikingly, a priest asks second officer King a question he finds ‘highly unusual’: when will Cook return to the ship to resume his former position, and how will he treat the crew left behind? This hints that Hawaiians might not have actually believed Cook was dead at all.

1:10:13 Cook's Historical Image Pivoted From Enlightenment Saint to Colonial Destroyer
Oil paintings from the 1780s–90s typically portrayed Cook standing alone on the beach, raising his hand to stop soldiers from shooting—the image of a ‘victim of his own humanity,’ depicted as a martyr to Enlightenment reason and compassion. But in contemporary times, especially in New Zealand, Hawaii, and Australia, the evaluation has completely reversed. Writer Anna Della Subin in 2022 called Cook a man who, ‘before becoming a god, was already burning entire villages and carving crosses on indigenous bodies’—characterizing him as an incarnation of colonial violence. The host reflects that they once defended Cook in 2023 but now recognizes that his loss of emotional control and behavioral contradictions during the third voyage make the ‘saint’ image untenable.

item.title: Churchill and Gandhi in the Boer War: who faced the cameras, who made the myths
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-empirehist-布尔战争里的查吉尔与甘地-谁在镜头前-谁在造神/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-26-empirehist-布尔战争里的查吉尔与甘地-谁在镜头前-谁在造神/
item.description: The Boer War was a media war. Baden-Powell and Churchill both became famous by exaggerating their roles in siege warfare. Gandhi carried stretchers to treat British soldiers because he believed loyalty to Britain would bring Indian freedom—a conviction he later publicly admitted was mistaken.
item.content:encoded:
The Boer War was a media war. Baden-Powell and Churchill both became famous by exaggerating their roles in siege warfare. Gandhi carried stretchers to treat British soldiers because he believed loyalty to Britain would bring Indian freedom—a conviction he later publicly admitted was mistaken.

It's worth listening to discover how much of the heroic narrative around Mafeking, Black Week, and Spionkop is real versus marketing; tactical military details can be fast-forwarded.

12:25 Mafeking's true saviors were the Batlaping, not Baden-Powell
The siege of Mafeking was portrayed in the British media as a Herculean feat, and Baden-Powell, with good PR instincts, exaggerated his role as ‘Mafeking's savior’. But much of the actual defense work was done by the Batlaping, who assisted the British. They sided with Britain over the Boers because they believed loyal service would earn them better treatment after the war—the same logic Gandhi would later follow in assisting the British.

17:36 Churchill's armored train heroics were probably exaggerated
The story goes that young war correspondent Churchill kept his composure during an ambush on his armored train, directing removal of wreckage to rescue casualties while taking fire. But Bill Nassau plainly stated, ‘I don't think that's what happened,’ arguing that Churchill was just a young reporter at the time, and only became this heroic figure through years of embellishment—even his later story of barefoot escape with thorns drawing blood is questionable. Fourteen-year-old diarist Frieda Schlossberg's records show that after Churchill's capture, he actually stayed in comfortable conditions at a prestigious model school, as a ‘privileged prisoner’.

22:54 Boer soldiers elected their officers and could vote to refuse battle
In the Boer command structure, officers were elected by soldiers, who could also vote on whether to participate in any given battle—if they thought it would mean senseless death, they could collectively vote to refuse. This highly democratic military setup explains why Louis Botha, at thirty-seven, was elected to replace a commanding officer who fell ill, and also explains why many Boer commandos would abandon their posts during siege to go home for weddings or cattle auctions, forcing commanders to resort to the whip for discipline—an early sign of the problems that would plague the Boer military later.

29:19 Lord Roberts at five-foot-three was the actual adult who turned the tide
Faced with Buller losing while eating corned beef sandwiches, the British replaced him with Lord Roberts, just five-foot-three but famous from the Indian Rebellion and the Afghan campaign. He had led troops on a three-week forced march of 313 miles from Kabul to Kandahar, and soldiers genuinely loved him—a stark contrast to Buller, who left them merely ‘not too displeased’. Kitchener joined at the same time, bringing the rigorous methodology of his engineering background, and their partnership was described as ‘finally, the adults have arrived’, marking when the British seriously began to redress the shame of Black Week.

34:29 Churchill immediately wired the newspaper a war assessment after escaping
Once aboard a ship bound for Durban, Churchill immediately wired the Morning Post a military assessment: a trained Boer fighter was worth four or five regular soldiers, modern rifles made frontal assault hopeless, and you'd need equally skilled riflemen or enormous numbers to suppress them—he estimated 250,000 troops, and noted that sending sufficient forces early would actually be cheaper. He also mocked English gentlemen for clinging to their fox-hunting saddles instead of coming to fight themselves.

38:35 Gandhi and Churchill probably passed each other at Spionkop without recognizing each other
After moving to Natal in 1893, Gandhi immediately faced racial discrimination. Following the famous Pietermaritzburg train incident, he founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894. When the Boer War broke out, he organized the Natal Indian Ambulance Corps, composed of 300 free Indians and 800 indentured sugar workers, serving as stretcher-bearers without compensation. At Spionkop, Gandhi and his team carried the wounded across several miles of rough terrain to field hospitals, while in the same battle Churchill was serving as a dispatch rider carrying messages up hillsides—the two may well have passed each other that day without either knowing who the other was.

40:47 Behind Gandhi's belief in British loyalty lay open racial contempt for Black Africans
Gandhi's assistance to the British aligned with his nonviolence principle, which explains why he chose to serve as a stretcher-bearer rather than take up arms. But the deeper motive was his then-belief that ‘proving loyalty would make the British grant you freedom’—a conviction he later publicly admitted was wrong. The show directly notes that Gandhi held open racial contempt for Black Africans during his South Africa years, believing Indians were superior to local Africans, and his opposition to the pass system was only to benefit Indian merchants and professionals like himself, not all people.

item.title: Awakening is not the endpoint—it opens the door to healing trauma
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-25-timferriss-禅师说-顿悟不是终点-它只是打开了疗愈童年创伤的门/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-25-timferriss-禅师说-顿悟不是终点-它只是打开了疗愈童年创伤的门/
item.description: At 19, a spontaneous awakening gave the author the joy of merging with all things, but six weeks later, returning home triggered a collapse into childhood trauma memories; the Zen master argues awakening merely opens the door to healing, not an endpoint.
item.content:encoded:
At 19, a spontaneous awakening gave the author the joy of merging with all things, but six weeks later, returning home triggered a collapse into childhood trauma memories; the Zen master argues awakening merely opens the door to healing, not an endpoint.

For those interested in meditation, poetry, Zen, and psychedelic therapy together. The episode isn't information-dense and has much casual conversation, but several segments on the aftereffects of awakening, the relationship between poetry and Zen, and the technical details of Jhana practice are worth listening to specifically.

17:23 Spontaneous awakening at 19 required no drugs or prior preparation
Henry Shukman describes how at 19, while traveling in South America, he suddenly experienced the dissolution of boundaries between self and world in a completely sober state without any psychedelic drugs.
